He rubbed at his arms, trying to work life back into the aching muscles. “Little well done for my tastes,” he muttered, flexing his fingers experimentally, “but it feels like everything’s still attached.” He glanced across the firelight to where Leon sat, looking very much like he too could use a nap. “You good?” Leon nodded, voice a little hoarse. “Yeah. Don’t remember much after the girls came in, but I’m no worse for wear.” Good. That was good. If Leon was coherent, then it had been worth it. Jake exhaled and dropped his head again, letting the dizziness ebb out with the fire’s warmth. “Fuck,” he muttered, “that was way worse than his usual mori. My head’s still ringing.” David’s hand settled on his shoulder, keeping him from tipping over as the world kept pitching gently around his head. “Yeah, that tracks. Doctor gets creative sometimes. Bastard’s never satisfied just running the script.” Across the fire, Felix let out a soft snort — dry and humorless. “That’s an understatement,” he muttered, something unreadable flickering behind his eyes. “Just take your time. The aftershocks’ll pass, but you’re probably gonna have trouble holding anything for a bit.” Jake flexed his fingers again, watching as they twitched and jumped slightly in response. He may have to stay off gens for a little while, at least until he could hold the wires without his arms trying to choreograph random interpretive dance in the delicate machinery. He sat in silence for a while, letting the trembling slowly bleed out of his limbs while David traced slow, grounding circles over his back. Creative , he thought bitterly, really was a fucking understatement. He’d taken his fair share of electric shocks before — burned synapses, short-circuited thoughts, the usual Fog-induced brain scrambles. Painful, sure, but fast. Rote. Survivable. This had been something else entirely. He could still hear the crack of bones locking under their own tension. Still feel the collapsing pressure in his chest, every muscle turning against him with surgical precision. Still smell the sheer, unfiltered panic as his body refused to obey anything but the torment it was drowning in. He clenched his jaw and shoved it down. He was safe. The trial was over. His people were here. That was what mattered. The memory would fade from his nerves — eventually. The Fog would see to that, whether he liked it or not. But that lingering taste, the knowledge of what had been done? That wasn’t going anywhere. Just another piece of trauma to be shelved, right alongside all the others. Jake exhaled, letting his head rest on his knees. And yet, even with everything he was trying not to think about, one weird detail kept itching at the edge of his thoughts. “Hey, Felix?” Jake’s voice cut through the quiet, still scratchy but steady. “Why would the Doctor tell me to say hi to you for him?” Felix went rigid, his grin falling, replaced by a haunted vacancy that made Jake’s stomach twist. To one side, Jake felt David's posture stiffen slightly with a nearly silent inhale. Jake blinked. “What?” he asked cautiously. “What happened?” Felix didn’t answer. His breath hitched — almost a flinch — before he surged to his feet and stormed off into the darker edges of the camp, muttering something sharp and half-German under his breath. Meg and Leon watched him go; curiosity blended with sympathy clear in their eyes. Claudette chased after him, earning a heated string of words for her trouble that left her frozen at the treeline, helpless as he vanished into the woods. Several nearby survivors who’d been lingering too close scattered in his wake, ducking behind trees and cover like startled animals, fleeing the direct fire of the oncoming warpath. Jake started to rise, guilt sparking fresh adrenaline through his limbs — but David’s hand clamped around his wrist and pulled him back down. “What...? What did I do?” "Let him go,” David sighed softly. “Felix and the Doc... those two have history." Jake stared after the direction Felix had gone, brow furrowed. “The fuck did the Doctor do to him?” David shook his head, turning back to the fire, poking at the edge of the flames like they held better answers. “He doesn’t like to talk about it,” he said finally. “And I’m not about to do it for him. We all got our issues here. Let’s leave it at that.” A sudden crash rang out in the distance — something getting kicked over hard — and Jake winced, his nerves tightening in sympathy. Whatever had happened to Felix... it hadn’t faded with the Fog. It was clearly still very raw. David didn’t look up. “Gotta say though,” he muttered, flipping a smoldering branch. “If the Doc took time to stab at Felix before going after you... you’re lucky you came back in the state you did.” Jake stared into the fire, watching the flames dance in silence as the distant echo of German curses was swallowed by the Fog. A heavy quiet settled over the group — unsettling in its stillness. He’d thought the trial couldn’t have been worse. Couldn’t have hurt more. But now... now he wasn’t so sure. His nerves still trembled faintly beneath his skin. The air tasted sharp, gritty. His lungs stung when he drew a full breath. His bones felt hollowed out from the strain and shock, still aching in ways the Fog hadn’t soothed yet — and might not for a while. If this was lucky... Then what the hell did unlucky look like? His gaze drifted to the shadows where Felix had disappeared. What the hell had happened between him and the Doctor? Jake exhaled slowly, the fire’s warmth doing little to chase the chill settling in his gut. Hopefully, he’d never have to find out.
